title: Can you change the scope (access modifier) of an overridden method, and what are the rules (widen only; private/static/final restrictions)?
shortTitle: Can you change the scope of an overridden method — widen only, private/static/final restrictions

s1_definition.profdef: YES, you can change the access modifier when overriding — but ONLY to WIDEN it (make MORE accessible). The order from narrow to wide: `private → default (package-private) → protected → public`. You can move RIGHT (widen) but NEVER LEFT (narrow). Parent has protected → child can make it public (wider) but NOT private (narrower). WHY: Liskov Substitution Principle — if code uses the parent reference and calls a protected method, replacing the parent object with a child object must still work. If the child narrows to private, that code breaks. Three methods CANNOT be overridden at all: `private` methods (not inherited — invisible to child), `static` methods (class-level, not instance-level — hidden, not overridden), `final` methods (explicitly sealed by the parent).
s1_definition.analogy: Head office publishes a procedure visible to all branches (protected). Mumbai branch can make it visible to EVERYONE (public) — more people can see it, which is fine. But Mumbai branch CANNOT make it visible to ONLY the branch manager (private) — that would break branches that already follow the procedure. If HO marks a procedure FINAL: no branch can modify it. If HO keeps a procedure PRIVATE: branches don't even know it exists. If it's a STATIC policy on the bank's website: branches can post their own version, but the bank website still shows HO's version (hidden, not overridden).
s1_definition.oneliner: Widen OK (protected→public). Narrow NOT OK (public→private). private = not inherited. static = hidden. final = sealed. Liskov: child must be at LEAST as accessible as parent.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** YES, you can change the access modifier when overriding — but ONLY to WIDEN it (make MORE accessible). The order from narrow to wide: `private → default (package-private) → protected → public`. You can move RIGHT (widen) but NEVER LEFT (narrow). Parent has protected → child can make it public (wider) but NOT private (narrower). WHY: Liskov Substitution Principle — if code uses the parent reference and calls a protected method, replacing the parent object with a child object must still work. If the child narrows to private, that code breaks. Three methods CANNOT be overridden at all: `private` methods (not inherited — invisible to child), `static` methods (class-level, not instance-level — hidden, not overridden), `final` methods (explicitly sealed by the parent).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Head office publishes a procedure visible to all branches (protected). Mumbai branch can make it visible to EVERYONE (public) — more people can see it, which is fine. But Mumbai branch CANNOT make it visible to ONLY the branch manager (private) — that would break branches that already follow the procedure. If HO marks a procedure FINAL: no branch can modify it. If HO keeps a procedure PRIVATE: branches don't even know it exists. If it's a STATIC policy on the bank's website: branches can post their own version, but the bank website still shows HO's version (hidden, not overridden).

**One line to remember:** Widen OK (protected→public). Narrow NOT OK (public→private). private = not inherited. static = hidden. final = sealed. Liskov: child must be at LEAST as accessible as parent.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The bank's internal transfer system has a protected `validate()` method on Account.** The external API needs this to be public for SavingsAccount (external partners call it). A developer tried to make it private for CurrentAccount (to hide validation from external callers) — compiler error. Another developer tried to override the static `getPolicy()` method — the override didn't work as expected (static hiding confused the team). The final `getBalance()` prevented a malicious subclass from returning fake balances. The test suite proves each rule with clear assertions.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Account has `protected void validate()`. SavingsAccount overrides with `public void validate()` — wider access. Code calling `account.validate()` through Account reference works because protected allows subclass access. SavingsAccount's public makes it EVEN MORE accessible — safe.

**Step 2.** If SavingsAccount tried `private void validate()` — narrower access — the compiler rejects it. Code that called `account.validate()` through Account reference (where validate is protected) would fail if the child's version were private. Liskov violated.

**Step 3.** `getAccountId()` is final. SavingsAccount CANNOT override it. Even a malicious subclass returning `"FAKE_ID"` is impossible. Final guarantees the behavior is sealed by the parent — critical for security-sensitive methods.

**Step 4.** `getPolicy()` is static. `SavingsAccount.getPolicy()` returns "Savings Special Policy." But `Account ref = new SavingsAccount(...); ref.getPolicy()` returns "Standard Banking Policy" — because static methods bind at COMPILE TIME to the variable type (Account), not the actual object type. No dynamic dispatch for static.

**Step 5.** `auditInternal()` is private in Account. SavingsAccount defines its OWN `auditInternal()` — but this is a COMPLETELY DIFFERENT method, not an override. `@Override` on it would cause a compile error: "does not override."
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ ACCESS MODIFIER OVERRIDE RULES ═══

  Parent modifier │ Child can use
  ────────────────│──────────────────────────────
  private          │ NOT INHERITED (child's same-name = NEW method)
  default          │ default ✅  protected ✅  public ✅
  protected        │ protected ✅  public ✅
  public           │ public ✅ ONLY

  Direction: → WIDEN only (more accessible). ← NARROW forbidden.

  ═══ CANNOT OVERRIDE ═══

  final method:   COMPILE ERROR — sealed by parent
  static method:  HIDDEN (compile-time binding to class, not dynamic dispatch)
  private method: NOT INHERITED (invisible to child)

  ═══ WHY (Liskov Substitution) ═══

  Account ref = new SavingsAccount(...);
  ref.validate();  // parent says: protected → accessible

  If child narrows to private: ref.validate() → FAILS! ❌ Liskov broken.
  If child widens to public: ref.validate() → WORKS! ✅ Even more accessible.
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
Access width order (narrow→wide):  private < default < protected < public
Rule: override may move RIGHT (widen), never LEFT (narrow).

┌────────────────────────────┐
│ AuthProcessor               │

│ #validate(Txn):boolean      │  protected (the contract floor)

└────────────────────────────┘

Why: caller coded against AuthProcessor expects ≥ parent access → LSP preserved.
private: not inherited → new method, not an override.
static/final: not polymorphically overridable.
SOLID: LSP (substitutability) enforced by compiler via access rules.
Call chain: Gateway → AuthProcessor ref → validate() → child impl (if accessible)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Yes, you can change the access modifier when overriding — but ONLY to widen it. The order from narrow to wide: private, default, protected, public. You can move right (widen) but never left (narrow). If the parent method is protected, the child can make it protected (same) or public (wider), but NOT default or private (narrower). If the parent method is public, the child MUST keep it public — it's already the widest. This rule exists because of Liskov Substitution: code written against the parent expects a certain accessibility level, and the child must maintain at LEAST that level.

Three methods cannot be overridden at all: private methods are not inherited — the child doesn't even know they exist. If the child declares a method with the same name, it's a completely new method. Static methods are class-level — they bind at compile time to the variable type, not the object type. A child can define a same-name static method, but this is METHOD HIDING, not overriding — no dynamic dispatch occurs. Final methods are explicitly sealed — the compiler prevents any child from changing their behavior.

In my access-modifier service, the static hiding is the most commonly confused rule. `Account ref = new SavingsAccount(...); ref.getPolicy()` returns "Standard Banking Policy" (Account's version), NOT "Savings Special Policy." If getPolicy were a normal instance method and overridden, it would return the child's version via dynamic dispatch. But static methods have NO dynamic dispatch — they bind to the COMPILE-TIME type of the variable. This is why static methods are "hidden," not "overridden" — an important distinction for interviews.
